name: United States
summary: US banks are supervised by a federal agency that depends on their charter: the OCC for national banks, the Federal Reserve for state member banks and holding companies, and the FDIC for state non-member banks. State banking departments such as NYDFS also supervise state-chartered and state-licensed institutions. FinCEN administers the Bank Secrecy Act, OFAC enforces sanctions, and the CFPB covers consumer financial law for banks above USD 10 billion in assets. Explicit training duties sit mainly in the BSA compliance program rules, the information security guidelines, the identity theft Red Flags rule, the mortgage loan originator rules and, for New York institutions, the DFS cybersecurity and transaction monitoring rules. In most other areas, examination manuals expect staff to be trained but do not prescribe a course.

regulators.name: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
regulators.role: Charters and supervises national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches of foreign banks; issues BSA program, safety and soundness and heightened standards rules.

regulators.name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
regulators.role: Supervises state member banks, bank holding companies and US operations of foreign banks; issues Regulation H (including the BSA compliance program rule) and SR supervisory letters.

regulators.name: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
regulators.role: Insures deposits and is the federal supervisor of state non-member banks; issues the BSA program rule in 12 CFR 326 and the Section 19 rules on persons with certain criminal records.

regulators.name: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
regulators.role: Treasury bureau that administers the Bank Secrecy Act: AML/CFT program, CIP, CDD and beneficial ownership, SAR, CTR and recordkeeping rules in 31 CFR Chapter X; runs the AML whistleblower program.

regulators.name: Office of Foreign Assets Control (US Department of the Treasury)
regulators.role: Administers and enforces US economic and trade sanctions, publishes the SDN List and sets blocking, rejection and reporting rules in 31 CFR Part 501.

regulators.name: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
regulators.role: Writes most federal consumer financial rules (e.g. Regulations B, E, P, Z) and supervises banks with more than USD 10 billion in assets for consumer law and UDAAP compliance.

regulators.name: Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council
regulators.role: Interagency body that publishes the common BSA/AML Examination Manual and IT Examination Handbook used by the federal banking agencies.

regulators.name: New York State Department of Financial Services
regulators.role: State regulator of New York-chartered and licensed banks and branches; issues the 23 NYCRR Part 500 cybersecurity and Part 504 transaction monitoring and filtering regulations.

regulators.name: US Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.role: Regulates securities markets, broker-dealers and investment advisers (including bank affiliates) and shares civil enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for issuers.

regulators.name: US Department of Justice
regulators.role: Prosecutes BSA, sanctions, bribery (including the FCPA and the Bank Bribery Act) and fraud offences; publishes its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs.

programs.title: United States | Bank Secrecy Act AML Compliance Program Training
audience: All bank employees in roles touched by the BSA
programs.why: Every bank's BSA/AML compliance program must contain four minimum elements, and one of them is training for appropriate personnel. The FinCEN rule and each federal banking agency's own rule say this, and examiners check it against the FFIEC manual. The manual expects role-tailored content, an overview for new hires, refreshers as rules change, and records of materials and attendance.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.210 Anti-money laundering program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: A bank meets the statutory AML program duty by keeping a program that includes internal controls, independent testing, a designated compliance person and training for appropriate personnel.

references.title: 12 CFR 21.21 Procedures for monitoring Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance
references.note: National banks and federal savings associations need a written, board-approved BSA program whose minimum elements include training for appropriate personnel.

references.title: 12 CFR 208.63 Procedures for monitoring Bank Secrecy Act compliance (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service)
references.note: State member banks must include training for appropriate personnel in their board-approved BSA compliance program.

references.title: 12 CFR 326.8 Bank Secrecy Act compliance
references.note: FDIC-supervised banks must provide training for appropriate personnel as one of four minimum program elements.

references.title: FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual: BSA/AML Training
references.note: Examiner guidance: tailor training to roles, brief new staff, train the board, update content for regulatory change, and keep training records.

programs.title: United States | Countering the Financing of Terrorism under the BSA and USA PATRIOT Act
audience: All bank employees in roles touched by the BSA
programs.why: Terrorist financing is in scope of the same BSA program and its required training element. Staff must recognise terrorism-related red flags, run CIP checks against government terrorist lists, and escalate cases for SAR filing. FinCEN's 2026 proposal would formally rename the program an AML/CFT program and describe an ongoing employee training program.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.210 Anti-money laundering program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: The program, including its training element, is the vehicle for both AML and CFT controls.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Programs (proposed rule)
references.note: Proposal to restate the program rule as an AML/CFT program focused on effectiveness; keeps ongoing employee training as a core pillar. Comments closed 9 June 2026; not final as of this review.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.220 Customer identification program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: The CIP must include procedures for checking customers against federal lists of known or suspected terrorists.

references.title: Fact Sheet: Proposed Rule to Fundamentally Reform Financial Institution AML/CFT Programs
references.note: The proposal keeps ongoing employee training as one of four required pillars, tailored in frequency and content to risk and role; not final as of this review.

programs.title: United States | Customer Identification Program (CIP)
programs.why: Banks must run a written, risk-based CIP inside the BSA program: collect name, date of birth, address and ID number, verify identity by documentary or non-documentary means, check government lists, give customer notice and keep records. The rule does not set a separate course, but staff opening accounts must know these procedures, and BSA training covers them.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.220 Customer identification program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Minimum CIP elements: identifying information, verification, failed-verification steps, recordkeeping, list checks, customer notice and reliance conditions.

references.title: 12 CFR 208.63 Procedures for monitoring Bank Secrecy Act compliance (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service)
references.note: The CIP is to be implemented as part of the BSA compliance program that includes the training element.

programs.title: United States | Customer Due Diligence (FinCEN CDD Rule)
programs.why: Since 2018 banks have had to include risk-based CDD procedures in the BSA program: understand the nature and purpose of customer relationships to build risk profiles, and identify and verify beneficial owners of legal entity customers. Staff who collect and assess this information need working knowledge of the rule. FinCEN eased some repeat-verification steps in 2026.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.230 Beneficial ownership requirements for legal entity customers (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Written procedures to identify and verify the beneficial owners (ownership and control prongs) of legal entity customers at account opening.

references.title: CDD Final Rule
references.note: FinCEN's landing page for the 2016 CDD rule, which added CDD as an explicit part of AML programs.

references.title: FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual
references.note: Contains the CDD and beneficial ownership examination sections used by all federal banking agencies.

programs.title: United States | Enhanced Due Diligence: Correspondent and Private Banking (Section 312)
programs.why: FinCEN requires special due diligence programs for correspondent accounts of foreign financial institutions and for private banking accounts of non-US persons, with enhanced steps for higher-risk foreign banks and for senior foreign political figures. Staff in these lines need specific knowledge to apply the enhanced checks and to know when to refuse, close or report an account.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.610 Due diligence programs for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions (FRRS copy)
references.note: Risk-based due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts, with enhanced steps for offshore-licensed or high-risk-jurisdiction banks.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.620 Due diligence programs for private banking accounts (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Identify owners, source of funds and purpose of private banking accounts and apply enhanced scrutiny where a senior foreign political figure is involved.

programs.title: United States | Ongoing Customer Due Diligence and Risk Profiles
programs.why: The CDD amendments to the program rule require ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions and, on a risk basis, to keep customer information up to date. Staff must know when events should trigger a review and how to update risk profiles.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.210 Anti-money laundering program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Includes risk-based procedures for ongoing CDD as part of the bank AML program.

references.title: CDD Rule FAQs
references.note: Consolidated FinCEN FAQs on beneficial ownership, updating customer information and risk-based ongoing monitoring, revised to reflect the February 2026 exceptive relief.

programs.title: United States | Beneficial Ownership: CDD Rule and Corporate Transparency Act Changes
programs.why: Banks still have to identify and verify the beneficial owners of legal entity customers under the CDD rule, even though Corporate Transparency Act filings to FinCEN are now limited to foreign reporting companies. Staff need to understand both the bank's own verification duty and why FinCEN's BOI registry will not hold data on most US companies.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.230 Beneficial ownership requirements for legal entity customers (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: 25 percent ownership prong plus one control person; banks may rely on customer certification unless they know of contrary facts.

references.title: Exceptive Relief from Requirement to Identify and Verify Beneficial Owners
references.note: FinCEN order relieving banks from re-identifying and re-verifying beneficial owners each time an existing customer opens a new account, subject to risk-based exceptions.

references.title: Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting Requirement Revision (final rule)
references.note: Makes permanent the 2025 exemption of US-formed companies and US persons from BOI reporting; only foreign reporting companies file.

references.title: FinCEN Permanently Ends Beneficial Ownership Reporting Requirements for Millions of Small Business Owners
references.note: FinCEN announcement of the final rule removing BOI reporting for US companies and US persons; foreign reporting companies still report foreign beneficial owners.

programs.title: United States | Senior Foreign Political Figures (PEP) Due Diligence
programs.why: US rules do not use a general PEP regime; the explicit duty is enhanced scrutiny of private banking accounts for non-US persons where a senior foreign political figure is an owner, aimed at detecting the proceeds of foreign corruption. Other PEP relationships are handled on a risk basis under CDD. Staff need to recognise these customers and apply the right level of scrutiny.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.620 Due diligence programs for private banking accounts (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Enhanced scrutiny of private banking accounts with a senior foreign political figure as nominal or beneficial owner.

references.title: Joint Statement on Bank Secrecy Act Due Diligence Requirements for Customers Who May Be Considered Politically Exposed Persons
references.issuer: Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, FinCEN, NCUA, OCC
references.note: Agencies clarify that PEP status alone does not require extra diligence beyond the risk-based CDD duty; diligence should follow risk.

programs.title: United States | Sanctions Screening and Blocking under OFAC Regulations
programs.why: All US persons, including banks, must block property of sanctioned persons, reject prohibited transactions and report them to OFAC within ten business days. The OFAC regulations do not prescribe training, but staff who screen, review alerts and process payments must understand these duties; the FDIC and FFIEC expect OFAC topics in BSA training.

references.title: 31 CFR 501.603 Reports of blocked, unblocked, or transferred blocked property
references.note: Reports of blocked property are due within ten business days through the OFAC Reporting System, with annual reports of blocked property held.

references.title: OFAC FAQs: Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
references.note: OFAC explains how banks block funds into segregated interest-bearing accounts and when they must reject instead; both blocked and rejected transactions are reported through the OFAC Reporting System within 10 business days.

references.title: RMS Manual of Examination Policies Section 8.1: Bank Secrecy Act, Anti-Money Laundering, and Office of Foreign Assets Control
references.note: FDIC examiner guidance lists OFAC policies among topics expected in operational staff training.

programs.title: United States | OFAC Framework for Compliance Commitments: Sanctions Training
audience: High-risk business lines (trade finance, payments, correspondent)
programs.why: OFAC's 2019 framework names training as one of five essential components of a sanctions compliance program, expects it at least annually, and asks for job-specific content and testing of understanding. It is guidance rather than a rule, but OFAC considers the existence and adequacy of a compliance program when deciding whether and how far to mitigate a civil penalty.

references.title: A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments
references.note: Training is one of five components; OFAC expects periodic training at least once a year, tailored to high-risk roles, with assessments.

programs.title: United States | Suspicious Activity Reporting (SAR) for Banks
programs.why: Banks must file a SAR within 30 days of first detecting a reportable transaction (generally USD 5,000 or more where they know or suspect illicit funds, BSA evasion or no lawful purpose), keep supporting records for five years, and keep SARs confidential. Staff must spot and escalate unusual activity and avoid tipping off; BSA training is where this knowledge is built.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.320 Reports by banks of suspicious transactions (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Sets reporting thresholds, the 30-day filing deadline (60 days if no suspect identified), five-year retention and SAR confidentiality.

references.title: SAR Frequently Asked Questions (October 2025)
references.note: Joint FinCEN and agency answers intended to cut defensive filing, e.g. activity near the CTR threshold alone does not require a SAR; continuing activity reviews and related timing.

programs.title: United States | Identifying Unusual Activity and Red Flags
programs.why: Bank SAR duties depend on front-line staff spotting unusual activity. FDIC and FFIEC examiners expect training for tellers, account opening, lending, wire room and IT staff on money laundering schemes, red flags and escalation routes. FinCEN advisories describe new typologies.

references.title: RMS Manual of Examination Policies Section 8.1: Bank Secrecy Act, Anti-Money Laundering, and Office of Foreign Assets Control
references.note: Lists the operational staff groups that should at least be trained and topics such as SAR and CTR procedures.

references.title: Alerts/Advisories/Notices/Bulletins/Fact Sheets
references.note: FinCEN typology advisories and alerts, a common source of red-flag training content.

programs.title: United States | Transaction Monitoring and Filtering (NYDFS Part 504)
audience: Model and data owners for monitoring systems
programs.why: For banks, branches and other institutions regulated by NYDFS, Part 504 requires a transaction monitoring program and a sanctions filtering program with defined features, including qualified staff and periodic training of stakeholders, plus a yearly board or senior officer compliance finding filed by 15 April. Banks outside New York achieve the same result through the BSA internal controls and training elements.

references.title: Transaction Monitoring Certification (3 NYCRR 504)
references.note: DFS page on Part 504: institutions keep monitoring and filtering programs and file an annual compliance certification for the prior year by 15 April, with supporting records kept for inspection.

references.title: DFS Issues Final Anti-Terrorism Transaction Monitoring and Filtering Program Regulation
references.note: DFS announcement of the final Part 504 rule, effective 1 January 2017; lists required program attributes, including qualified personnel and periodic training on the monitoring and filtering program.

programs.title: United States | Correspondent Banking AML (31 CFR 1010.610 and Section 311/313 Measures)
audience: Correspondent banking and financial institutions group
programs.why: US banks must apply risk-based due diligence to every correspondent account they maintain for a foreign financial institution and enhanced diligence for higher-risk foreign banks. FinCEN advisories also tell them to apply extra diligence for jurisdictions on FATF lists. Correspondent staff need specialist knowledge of these steps and of the shell bank prohibition.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.610 Due diligence programs for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions (FRRS copy)
references.note: General and enhanced due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts, periodic review and steps when diligence fails.

references.title: 31 CFR 1010.630 Prohibition on correspondent accounts for foreign shell banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Banks may not keep correspondent accounts for foreign shell banks and must take reasonable steps to stop foreign bank correspondents from passing services on to shell banks.

programs.title: United States | Risk-Based BSA/AML Program and the 2026 Effectiveness Proposal
programs.why: Federal supervisors expect BSA programs to be built on the bank's own risk assessment. FinCEN's April 2026 proposal, with parallel proposals from the banking agencies, would require a documented risk assessment process and judge programs on whether they are both established and maintained effectively. Compliance and business staff need to understand risk-based judgements.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Programs (proposed rule)
references.note: Would restate program requirements around risk assessment and effectiveness; comments closed 9 June 2026; final rule pending at review.

references.title: Fact Sheet: Proposed Rule to Fundamentally Reform Financial Institutions' AML/CFT Programs
references.note: FinCEN summary of the 2026 proposal, which replaces the withdrawn 2024 proposal.

references.title: FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual
references.note: Examiners scope reviews from the bank's BSA/AML risk assessment.

programs.title: United States | BSA Recordkeeping, CTR and Funds Transfer Records
programs.why: Banks must make and keep specified records, including originator and beneficiary details for funds transfers of USD 3,000 or more, and file currency transaction reports. CIP, beneficial ownership and SAR records each have five-year retention periods. Operations staff need to know what to capture and how long to keep it.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.410 Records to be made and retained by banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Funds transfer recordkeeping for transfers of USD 3,000 or more, including identification of non-established customers.

references.title: 31 CFR Part 1020 Rules for Banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: Bank-specific program, reporting (including CTR exemptions) and recordkeeping rules.

programs.title: United States | BSA/AML Training for Branch and Frontline Staff
programs.why: The program rules require training for appropriate personnel, and examiners read that to cover, at minimum, operational staff such as tellers, new accounts, lending and wire room. Frontline content should cover CIP, cash reporting, structuring, red flags and internal escalation, adjusted to each role.

references.title: 12 CFR 326.8 Bank Secrecy Act compliance
references.note: Training for appropriate personnel is a required program element.

references.title: RMS Manual of Examination Policies Section 8.1: Bank Secrecy Act, Anti-Money Laundering, and Office of Foreign Assets Control
references.note: Says training must reach at least operational staff such as tellers, new accounts, lending, bookkeeping, wire room, international and IT staff, with a BSA overview for new employees.

references.title: FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual: BSA/AML Training
references.note: Training should be tailored to each person's responsibilities, with an overview for new staff.

references.title: 31 CFR 1020.210 Anti-money laundering program requirements for banks (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service copy)
references.note: FinCEN rule for all banks: the AML program must include training for appropriate personnel.

programs.title: United States | BSA/AML Oversight for Boards and Senior Management
programs.why: Each agency's rule requires the board to approve the BSA program, and examiners expect directors and senior managers to know enough about BSA risks and requirements to oversee it and fund it adequately. The FFIEC manual says the board should receive foundational training, but no separate course is prescribed by rule.

references.title: 12 CFR 21.21 Procedures for monitoring Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance
references.note: The written BSA program must be approved by the board and noted in the minutes.

references.title: FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual: BSA/AML Training
references.note: Directors and senior management should receive training appropriate to their oversight role.

references.title: 12 CFR 208.63 Procedures for monitoring Bank Secrecy Act compliance (Federal Reserve Regulatory Service)
references.note: The written BSA compliance program must be approved by the board of directors and noted in the minutes.

references.title: RMS Manual of Examination Policies Section 8.1: Bank Secrecy Act, Anti-Money Laundering, and Office of Foreign Assets Control
references.note: FDIC examiners expect banks to keep executives and directors informed of BSA changes and to give directors and officers adequate BSA training.

programs.title: United States | Anti-Bribery: Bank Bribery Act and FCPA
programs.why: The Bank Bribery Act makes it a crime for bank insiders to seek or accept anything of value in connection with bank business, and the FCPA prohibits bribing foreign officials. The FDIC asks banks to put these rules in a code of conduct with periodic training. DOJ prosecutors check whether training is tailored to risk and tested for effectiveness. Neither statute itself prescribes training.

references.title: Corporate Codes of Conduct: Guidance on Implementing an Effective Ethics Program (FIL-105-2005)
references.note: Recommends codes covering bank bribery and conflicts, written acknowledgement by staff and periodic training.

references.title: Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs
references.issuer: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division
references.note: Prosecutors assess risk-based, tailored training and how a company measures its effectiveness; used in FCPA and other corporate cases.

programs.title: United States | Identity Theft Red Flags and Fraud Prevention
audience: Call centre and card servicing staff
programs.why: Banks holding consumer or other covered accounts must run a written Identity Theft Prevention Program, approved by the board, that detects and responds to red flags. One required element of administering the program is to train staff as necessary to implement it effectively. The rule sets no frequency, so training follows the bank's needs and changes in risk.

references.title: 12 CFR 41.90 Duties regarding the detection, prevention, and mitigation of identity theft
references.note: Program administration must include training staff, as necessary, to implement the program; parallel rules apply for other agencies.

references.title: 12 CFR 222.90 Duties regarding the detection, prevention, and mitigation of identity theft (Federal Reserve)
references.note: Federal Reserve version of the Red Flags rule: administering the program includes board approval, senior oversight and training staff, as necessary, to implement it effectively.

references.title: Appendix J to Part 222: Interagency Guidelines on Identity Theft Detection, Prevention, and Mitigation (Federal Reserve)
references.note: Interagency guidelines, identical across the agencies, with red flag categories and guidance on building and administering the program.

references.title: Fighting Identity Theft with the Red Flags Rule: A How-To Guide for Business
references.note: Plain-language guide; notes that employees at many levels play a role in detection.

programs.title: United States | OCC Heightened Standards: Ongoing Director Training
audience: Directors of covered large national banks
programs.why: The OCC's heightened standards guidelines require the board of a covered large bank to establish and follow a formal, ongoing training program for all directors. The program must reflect each director's experience and the bank's risk profile and cover complex products, risks and applicable laws. The OCC has proposed raising the coverage threshold sharply.

references.title: Appendix D to Part 30: OCC Guidelines Establishing Heightened Standards for Certain Large Insured National Banks, Insured Federal Savings Associations, and Insured Federal Branches
references.note: Board must establish and adhere to a formal, ongoing training program for all directors, shaped by their knowledge and the bank's risk profile.

references.title: OCC Guidelines Establishing Heightened Standards: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Bulletin 2025-51)
references.note: Proposes raising the asset threshold for coverage from USD 50 billion to USD 700 billion.

programs.title: United States | Section 19 FDI Act and Suitability of Bank Personnel
programs.why: The US has no general fit-and-proper regime for bank staff. Section 19 of the FDI Act bars people convicted of certain dishonesty, breach of trust or money laundering offences from working in an insured bank without FDIC consent. Agencies also review new directors and senior officers in some cases. HR and managers need to know the screening rules when hiring.

references.title: 12 CFR Part 303 Subpart L: Section 19 of the FDI Act (Consent to Service of Persons Convicted of, or Who Have Program Entries for, Certain Criminal Offenses)
references.note: Explains who is covered, which offences trigger the bar, de minimis exemptions and how to apply for consent.

references.title: Section 19 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act
references.note: FDIC page on Section 19 consent applications; subpart L was revised to reflect the Fair Hiring in Banking Act by a final rule effective 1 October 2024.

programs.title: United States | Code of Conduct, Conflicts of Interest and Ethics
programs.why: Supervisors expect banks to keep a code of conduct covering bank bribery, self-dealing, gifts and conflicts of interest, to have staff sign acknowledgements, and to train them periodically. This is supervisory guidance rather than a rule-based training obligation.

references.title: Corporate Codes of Conduct: Guidance on Implementing an Effective Ethics Program (FIL-105-2005)
references.note: Recommends signed acknowledgements, periodic training and consistent enforcement of the code.

programs.title: United States | AML and Sanctions Whistleblower Protections
programs.why: The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 created a FinCEN whistleblower award and anti-retaliation regime for reports of BSA and sanctions violations. FinCEN proposed implementing rules in April 2026 and will pay awards once they are final. Banks should make sure staff know how to raise concerns and that managers do not retaliate. No training duty has been verified.

references.title: Whistleblower Program
references.note: Describes the AML and sanctions whistleblower program; awards will be processed and paid once the implementing rule, proposed on 1 April 2026, is final.

programs.title: United States | Consumer Compliance Management System (CFPB and Federal Banking Agencies)
programs.why: Consumer examiners assess whether a bank's compliance management system includes current, role-specific training kept up to date with new products and rule changes, alongside policies, monitoring and complaint response. Weak training is a common examination finding. The law itself does not prescribe a separate course.

references.title: CFPB Supervision and Examination Manual: Compliance Management Review
references.note: Training is a reviewed component of the compliance management system; examiners check content, completion and updates.

references.title: Comptroller's Handbook: Compliance Management Systems
references.note: OCC examiner expectations for the consumer compliance management system, including training.

programs.title: United States | Fair Lending: ECOA and Regulation B
programs.why: ECOA and Regulation B forbid credit discrimination on prohibited bases and set rules on applications, adverse action notices and data collection. Examiners review training on fair lending as part of compliance management. In April 2026 the CFPB amended Regulation B to remove disparate impact (the effects test) and narrow discouragement, effective 21 July 2026, so content needs updating.

references.title: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) examination procedures
references.note: CFPB ECOA procedures, updated July 2026 for the April 2026 Regulation B amendments that removed the effects test (disparate impact), narrowed discouragement and restricted special purpose credit programs.

programs.title: United States | UDAAP and Accurate Product Disclosure
programs.why: Federal law prohibits unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices in consumer finance, and a practice can breach UDAAP even when it meets disclosure rules such as TILA. Examiners look at the net impression of marketing and at whether staff are trained to describe products accurately.

references.title: CFPB Examination Procedures: Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices
references.note: Explains the unfairness, deception and abusiveness standards and how examiners review marketing, disclosures and controls.

programs.title: United States | Regulation E: Electronic Fund Transfer Rights and Error Resolution
programs.why: Regulation E gives consumers rights over electronic transfers, including limits on liability for unauthorised transfers and strict timelines to investigate errors, give provisional credit and report results. Staff who take customer complaints must recognise an error notice, even an oral one, and start the process on time.

references.title: 12 CFR 1005.11 Procedures for resolving errors
references.note: Defines errors and sets investigation, provisional credit and notice deadlines.

references.title: 12 CFR Part 1005 Electronic Fund Transfers (Regulation E)
references.note: Full text of Regulation E, including remittance transfer rules.

programs.title: United States | Consumer Complaint Handling
programs.why: Complaint response is a core part of the compliance management system that CFPB and agency examiners review. Banks should capture, route and fix complaints and use them to find root causes, which requires staff to recognise and escalate complaints. Specific rules such as Regulation E add deadlines.

references.title: CFPB Supervision and Examination Manual: Compliance Management Review
references.note: Consumer complaint response is one of the reviewed components alongside training.

programs.title: United States | Sales Practices and Prevention of Unauthorised Account Openings
programs.why: After sales-practice scandals, examiners look closely at incentive-driven selling. The CFPB compliance management review expects training on ethical standards, risky behaviours, accurate disclosure and evidence of consumer consent for new products and upselling. UDAAP is the underlying legal standard.

references.title: CFPB Supervision and Examination Manual: Compliance Management Review
references.note: Includes review of sales practices training, consent evidence and incentive controls.

references.title: CFPB Examination Procedures: Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices
references.note: UDAAP standards used to assess misleading or abusive selling.

programs.title: United States | GLBA Financial Privacy (Regulation P)
programs.why: Regulation P requires initial and, in many cases, annual privacy notices and lets consumers opt out of certain sharing with non-affiliated third parties. Staff who handle customer data or marketing need to know these limits; the related security guidelines require trained staff.

references.title: 12 CFR Part 1016 Privacy of Consumer Financial Information (Regulation P)
references.note: Privacy notice, opt-out and redisclosure rules for banks and other financial institutions.

programs.title: United States | Mortgage Loan Originator Qualification and Training (Regulation Z and SAFE Act)
audience: Mortgage loan originators employed by banks
programs.why: Bank-employed mortgage loan originators must be registered under the SAFE Act. Their employer must screen them and give periodic training on the federal and state law that applies to their lending. Training must be timely and suit their duties, and NMLS-approved continuing education can count. Licensed non-bank originators face pre-licensing and yearly continuing education.

references.title: 12 CFR 1026.36 Prohibited acts or practices and certain requirements for credit secured by a dwelling
references.note: Loan originator organisations must screen individual originators who are not required to be licensed and give them periodic training on the federal and state law that applies to their origination work.

references.title: Official Interpretation to 1026.36
references.note: Explains frequency, tailoring and use of NMLS-approved courses for originator training.

programs.title: United States | GLBA Information Security Program: Staff Training
programs.why: The Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards require each bank to train staff to implement its information security program. The FFIEC Information Security booklet expects ongoing awareness communications and confirmation that employees complete training each year.

references.title: Appendix B to Part 364: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: Among risk controls, banks must train staff to implement the information security program; parallel appendices exist for OCC (Part 30) and Federal Reserve (Part 208).

references.title: Appendix B to Part 30: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: OCC version of the same guidelines for national banks.

references.title: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards (12 CFR 208, Appendix D-2; Federal Reserve Regulatory Service)
references.note: As part of managing and controlling risk, the bank must train staff to implement its information security program; the text is common to all three banking agencies.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Information Security
references.note: Expects security awareness training with annual completion by employees and role training for technical staff.

programs.title: United States | NYDFS Part 500 Cybersecurity Awareness Training
audience: All personnel of NYDFS-regulated banks and branches
programs.why: NYDFS-regulated institutions, including New York-chartered banks and branches of foreign banks, must give all personnel cybersecurity awareness training at least once a year. It must cover social engineering and be updated for risks found in the risk assessment. Federal rules require trained staff but set no annual cyber course; many banks adopt the NYDFS standard nationwide.

references.title: Cybersecurity Regulation 23 NYCRR Part 500
references.note: Periodic, at least annual, cybersecurity awareness training including social engineering for all personnel, updated for risks found in the risk assessment; applied 180 days after the November 2023 amendment.

references.title: Part 500 Requirement Checklist for DFS-Regulated Entities with 500.19(a) Limited Exemptions
references.note: DFS checklist for smaller entities with a limited exemption; lists the annual duties, including at least annual awareness training with social engineering for all staff.

programs.title: United States | Cybersecurity Risk Management (FFIEC IT Handbook and NYDFS Part 500)
programs.why: Federal guidelines require a board-overseen information security program, and the FFIEC handbook sets examiner expectations for governance, risk assessment and controls. NYDFS Part 500 adds a CISO, board reporting and role training for security staff. Those running the program must be competent in it, though no single course is prescribed.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook InfoBase
references.note: Examination booklets on information security, management, architecture and operations.

references.title: Cybersecurity Regulation 23 NYCRR Part 500
references.note: Requires a cybersecurity program, a CISO and board oversight, and cybersecurity updates and training for cybersecurity personnel.

programs.title: United States | Phishing and Social Engineering Awareness (NYDFS Part 500)
programs.why: Since the 2023 amendments, NYDFS requires annual awareness training that specifically covers social engineering. The FFIEC also points to phishing tests as a way to measure training effectiveness. Phishing and business email compromise remain major causes of losses and incidents at US banks.

references.title: Cybersecurity Regulation 23 NYCRR Part 500
references.note: Annual awareness training must include social engineering.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Information Security
references.note: Awareness training and communications expected for all staff.

programs.title: United States | Computer-Security Incident Notification (36-Hour Rule)
programs.why: Banking organisations must notify their primary federal regulator within 36 hours of determining that a notification incident has occurred, and bank service providers must alert bank customers of material disruptions. NYDFS sets its own 72-hour notice. Incident teams must know how to classify incidents and who reports them.

references.title: Computer-Security Incident Notification Requirements for Banking Organizations and Their Bank Service Providers (86 FR 66424)
references.note: Joint final rule: notify the primary federal regulator no later than 36 hours after determining a notification incident has occurred; service providers must alert bank customers of disruptions of four hours or more. Compliance from 1 May 2022.

references.title: Computer-Security Incident Notification: Final Rule (Bulletin 2021-55)
references.note: OCC summary of the rule; compliance from 1 May 2022.

programs.title: United States | Customer Information Security Incidents and Breach Response
programs.why: Under the GLBA security guidelines, banks must protect customer information and respond to unauthorised access, including notifying regulators and, where misuse is likely, affected customers. State breach laws and the 36-hour rule add duties. Teams handling breaches must know these steps.

references.title: Appendix B to Part 364: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: Security program duties for customer information, with supplementary guidance on response programs for unauthorised access.

references.title: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: Federal Reserve small-entity compliance guide to the security guidelines; covers staff training under paragraph III.C.2 and response programs for unauthorised access.

programs.title: United States | Operational Resilience (Interagency Sound Practices)
programs.why: The 2020 interagency paper sets out sound practices for the largest banks to stay resilient against cyber, pandemic and other disruptions: governance, scenario analysis, third-party risk, mapping of critical operations and secure IT. It creates no new rule, but supervisors expect management to apply it. The Federal Reserve reposted it in June 2026 with references to reputational risk removed.

references.title: SR 20-24: Interagency Paper on Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience
references.note: Joint sound practices for the largest firms; the Federal Reserve revised the attachment on 2 June 2026 to remove references to reputational risk.

references.title: Operational Risk: Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience (Bulletin 2020-94)
references.note: OCC transmittal of the same paper.

programs.title: United States | IT Risk Management (FFIEC IT Examination Handbook)
programs.why: The FFIEC IT Examination Handbook sets common examiner expectations for IT governance, risk management, development, operations and audit. Its management booklet treats awareness and training as support for IT and security policies. Those managing technology risk need to know these expectations.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook InfoBase
references.note: Interagency IT examination booklets.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Management
references.note: IT governance and risk management expectations, including awareness and training.

programs.title: United States | Enterprise Risk Management: Regulation YY Risk Committee and Chief Risk Officer
audience: Chief risk officer and risk management staff
Senior management of large banking organizations
programs.why: Large bank holding companies must run an enterprise-wide risk management framework overseen by a board risk committee and a chief risk officer, and the rule sets experience requirements for both roles rather than a training course. Programs that build the knowledge these roles need, and that explain the framework to business line managers, support that duty. Large national banks also follow the OCC heightened standards (see program 35), which the OCC proposed in December 2025 to narrow to much larger banks.

references.title: 12 CFR 252.33 Risk-management and risk committee requirements (Regulation YY, FRRS copy)
references.note: Covered large bank holding companies need a board risk committee with at least one member experienced in managing the risks of large, complex firms, and a chief risk officer with that kind of experience who oversees enterprise-wide limits and the risk framework.

programs.title: United States | Liquidity Risk Management: Regulation YY and the Interagency Policy Statement
programs.why: Large bank holding companies must have the board set a liquidity risk tolerance at least once a year, have the risk committee approve the contingency funding plan, and keep an independent review of liquidity risk management at least annually. Smaller banks are expected to follow the 2010 interagency policy statement on cash flow projections, diverse funding, stress testing, liquid asset cushions and contingency funding plans. Neither text prescribes training, but staff who run these processes must understand them.

references.title: 12 CFR 252.34 Liquidity risk-management requirements (Regulation YY, FRRS copy)
references.note: The board approves the liquidity risk tolerance at least annually, the risk committee approves the contingency funding plan, and an independent function reviews liquidity risk management at least once a year.

references.title: SR 10-6 Interagency Policy Statement on Funding and Liquidity Risk Management
references.note: Sets out supervisory expectations for identifying, measuring, monitoring and controlling funding and liquidity risk, with emphasis on cash flow projections, funding diversity, stress tests, liquid assets and a contingency funding plan.

programs.title: United States | Interest Rate Risk Management (Interagency Advisory)
audience: Risk management and model validation staff
programs.why: The federal banking agencies expect every insured bank to have active board and senior management oversight of interest rate risk and a full process to measure, monitor and control it, including stress scenarios well beyond the expected path of rates. This is supervisory guidance, not a training rule, but asset-liability staff and committee members need the knowledge to run and challenge the measurement.

references.title: SR 10-1 Interagency Advisory on Interest Rate Risk
references.note: Reminds institutions of sound practices for interest rate risk, stressing board and senior management oversight and a risk management process that measures, monitors and controls exposure.

programs.title: United States | Regulatory Capital Rules (Regulation Q and the 2026 Capital Proposals)
programs.why: Banks must hold minimum risk-based and leverage capital ratios, and community banks may opt into the simpler community bank leverage ratio, which the agencies lowered from 9 to 8 percent from 1 July 2026. In March 2026 the agencies proposed recalibrating standardized risk weights and a new expanded risk-based approach for the largest firms. Staff who calculate, report and plan capital need to keep up with these changes; the rules set no training duty.

references.title: 12 CFR 217.10 Minimum capital requirements (Regulation Q, FRRS copy)
references.note: Sets the minimum common equity tier 1, tier 1, total capital and leverage ratios for Board-regulated institutions and refers to the community bank leverage ratio option.

references.title: Regulatory Capital Rule: Community Bank Leverage Ratio Framework (final rule)
references.issuer: OCC, Federal Reserve Board and FDIC
references.note: Lowers the community bank leverage ratio requirement to 8 percent and lengthens the grace period for banks that stop meeting the qualifying criteria.

references.title: Regulatory Capital Rules: Regulatory Capital and Standardized Approach for Risk-Weighted Assets (proposed rule)
references.issuer: OCC, Federal Reserve Board and FDIC
references.note: Proposes recalibrated standardized risk weights and recognition of most accumulated other comprehensive income for Category III and IV firms; comments closed 18 June 2026.

programs.title: United States | Stress Testing and Capital Planning (Regulation YY and Capital Plan Rule)
audience: Capital planning and stress testing teams
programs.why: Bank holding companies with USD 100 billion or more in assets must submit capital plans and are given a stress capital buffer, and covered firms must run company-run stress tests on a set annual or two-yearly cycle. In October 2026 the Federal Reserve finalised averaging of two years of stress test results for the buffer (effective 1 December 2026) and a separate rule on publishing its models and scenarios. Teams running these processes need current knowledge of the rules; no training duty is set.

references.title: 12 CFR 252.54 Stress test (Regulation YY, FRRS copy)
references.note: Covered companies must conduct company-run stress tests, annually for the largest categories and every other year for others, on data as of the prior year end.

references.title: 12 CFR 225.8 Capital planning and stress capital buffer requirement (Regulation Y, FRRS copy)
references.note: Applies capital planning and the stress capital buffer to US bank holding companies with average total consolidated assets of USD 100 billion or more and to certain intermediate holding companies.

references.title: Modifications to the Capital Plan Rule and Stress Capital Buffer Requirement (final rule)
references.note: Bases the stress capital buffer on the average of the two most recent supervisory stress tests and moves its annual effective date to 1 January.

programs.title: United States | Model Risk Management (Revised Interagency Guidance, SR 26-2)
audience: Senior management of banks over USD 30 billion
programs.why: In April 2026 the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC replaced SR 11-7 and the 2021 BSA/AML model statement with revised, risk-based model risk guidance aimed mainly at banking organizations above USD 30 billion in assets. It expects effective challenge by people with the right expertise, independence and standing, and sound validation, but states that it sets no enforceable standards. Training of model users, developers and validators is good practice under it.

references.title: SR 26-2 Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management
references.note: Issues the revised interagency model risk guidance and states that it supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8.

references.title: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (attachment to SR 26-2)
references.issuer: Federal Reserve Board, OCC and FDIC
references.note: Describes a risk-based approach to model governance, development, validation and vendor models; effective challenge needs appropriate expertise and independence; the guidance is not enforceable in itself.

programs.title: United States | Third-Party Relationships: Interagency Risk Management Guidance
programs.why: The 2023 interagency guidance covers the life cycle of third-party relationships, including fintech partnerships: planning, due diligence, contract terms, ongoing monitoring and exit. Banks stay responsible for outsourced activities, so staff who own vendor relationships need to know these expectations.

references.title: Third-Party Relationships: Interagency Guidance on Risk Management (Bulletin 2023-17)
references.note: Joint guidance that replaced each agency's earlier third-party and outsourcing guidance.

references.title: SR 23-4: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management
references.note: Federal Reserve transmittal; states the guidance imposes no new requirements.

programs.title: United States | Business Continuity Management (FFIEC BCM Booklet)
programs.why: The FFIEC Business Continuity Management booklet expects a continuity training program for all stakeholders. It should be risk-based, planned over several years and tailored to each audience, and backed by exercises and tests at suitable intervals. It is examiner guidance, not a rule.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Business Continuity Management, Section VI Training
references.note: Management should run a business continuity training program covering the board, management, process owners and staff.

references.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Business Continuity Management, Section VII Exercises and Tests
references.note: Exercises and tests should validate plans at suitable intervals and after significant change.

programs.title: United States | Resolution Planning (Regulation QQ and FDIC IDI Rule)
programs.why: The largest bank holding companies must file resolution plans with the Federal Reserve and FDIC on a fixed cycle, and large insured banks file separate resolution submissions with the FDIC, which proposed in June 2026 to raise the threshold and slim the content. The OCC rescinded its recovery planning guidelines with effect from 1 May 2026. Staff who maintain these plans need to know the requirements; no training is prescribed.

references.title: 12 CFR 243.4 Resolution plan required (Regulation QQ, FRRS copy)
references.note: Global systemically important bank holding companies and certain other firms file resolution plans with the Board and the FDIC every two years; other covered firms file on longer cycles.

references.title: Resolution Submissions Required for Covered Insured Depository Institutions (proposed rule)
references.note: Proposes a higher, indexed threshold, narrower content and an end to credibility assessments and capabilities testing for insured bank resolution submissions; comments closed 31 August 2026.

references.title: Rescission of OCC Guidelines Establishing Standards for Recovery Planning (final rule)
references.note: The OCC withdrew its recovery planning guidelines for large national banks and federal savings associations with effect from 1 May 2026.

programs.title: United States | Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage Rule (Regulation Z)
programs.why: Before making most closed-end residential mortgage loans a creditor must make a reasonable, good-faith determination, based on verified information, that the consumer can repay. Underwriters must apply the required factors and the qualified mortgage conditions correctly. In 2026 the CFPB and Federal Reserve also reminded lenders to weigh income stability for borrowers not authorised to work in the US. The rule sets no training duty, but underwriting staff need this knowledge.

references.title: 12 CFR 1026.43 Minimum standards for transactions secured by a dwelling (Regulation Z)
references.note: A creditor may not make a covered mortgage loan without a reasonable, good-faith determination at or before consummation that the consumer can repay it under its terms.

references.title: SR 26-4 Guidance on Lending to Individuals Not Legally Authorized to Work in the United States
references.note: Reminds supervised banks that underwriting should consider how uncertain work authorisation may affect income stability, repayment capacity and collateral recovery.

references.title: Statement on Ability To Repay and Immigration Status
references.note: CFPB statement reminding creditors of their ability-to-repay duties under Regulation Z.

programs.title: United States | Loan Accommodations, Workouts and Mortgage Loss Mitigation
audience: Mortgage servicing and loss mitigation staff
programs.why: The agencies expect banks to work prudently with creditworthy commercial borrowers in difficulty and set out how loan accommodations and workouts should be analysed and classified. For residential mortgages, Regulation X requires servicers to keep policies and procedures so that personnel can identify every loss mitigation option and properly evaluate borrowers. These texts call for knowledgeable staff rather than a specific course.

references.title: SR 23-5 Prudent Commercial Real Estate Loan Accommodations and Workouts
references.note: Interagency policy statement on working constructively with commercial borrowers who cannot meet current terms, with principles for analysing and classifying modified loans.

references.title: 12 CFR 1024.38 General servicing policies, procedures, and requirements (Regulation X)
references.note: Servicers must keep procedures that let their personnel identify all loss mitigation options, access borrower documents promptly and evaluate borrowers properly.

programs.title: United States | Allowances for Credit Losses (CECL Interagency Policy Statement)
audience: Credit risk and allowance modelling staff
programs.why: US banks that report under GAAP measure expected credit losses using the CECL methodology. The interagency policy statement, revised in 2023 to remove references to troubled debt restructurings, sets supervisory expectations for allowance processes, documentation, governance and validation. IFRS 9 does not apply to US banks. Staff who estimate and review the allowance need current knowledge; no training duty is set.

references.title: SR 20-12 Interagency Policy Statement on Allowances for Credit Losses (revised April 2023)
references.note: Describes measurement of expected credit losses under CECL and supervisory expectations for allowance processes; revised in 2023 to align with the removal of TDR accounting.

programs.title: United States | Real Estate Appraisals and Evaluations (FIRREA Appraisal Rules)
audience: Appraisal management and collateral valuation staff
Credit officers ordering appraisals or evaluations
programs.why: Real estate-related transactions above set thresholds need an appraisal by a state-certified or state-licensed appraiser, and every staff or fee appraiser on a federally related transaction must hold that certification or licence. Competence for a particular assignment must also rest on the appraiser's education and experience, not the licence alone. The 2010 interagency guidelines add expectations for independence, review and evaluations below the thresholds.

references.title: 12 CFR 225.66 Professional association membership; competency (Regulation Y, FRRS copy)
references.note: All staff and fee appraisers on federally related transactions must be state-certified or state-licensed, and competence for each assignment is judged on experience and education.

references.title: 12 CFR 225.63 Appraisals required; transactions requiring a state-certified or -licensed appraiser (FRRS copy)
references.note: Lists the real estate-related transactions that need an appraisal by a certified or licensed appraiser and the exemptions, such as residential transactions of USD 400,000 or less.

references.title: SR 10-16 Interagency Appraisal and Evaluation Guidelines
references.note: Interagency guidance on a prudent appraisal and evaluation program, covering independence, minimum standards, evaluations and review.

programs.title: United States | Credit Reporting: FCRA Furnisher Accuracy and Integrity (Regulation V)
audience: Credit reporting and data quality staff
programs.why: Banks that furnish consumer information to credit bureaus must keep written policies and procedures on its accuracy and integrity, review them periodically, and consider the interagency guidelines, adopting those that fit. The guidelines list training of staff involved in furnishing as one component to address where appropriate. Because training is a guideline to be weighed rather than an absolute rule, this is classed as competence, though most banks do train these staff.

references.title: 12 CFR 1022.42 Reasonable policies and procedures concerning the accuracy and integrity of furnished information (FRRS copy)
references.note: Furnishers must have written accuracy and integrity procedures, must consider the Appendix E guidelines and adopt those that are appropriate, and must review the procedures periodically.

references.title: Appendix E to Part 1022 Interagency Guidelines Concerning the Accuracy and Integrity of Information Furnished to Consumer Reporting Agencies
references.note: Among the components a furnisher should address as appropriate is training staff who take part in furnishing so they can apply the policies and procedures.

programs.title: United States | Mortgage Servicing Policies and Procedures (Regulation X)
audience: Customer service and loss mitigation staff
programs.why: Mortgage servicers must keep policies and procedures reasonably designed to give accurate information, evaluate loss mitigation properly, oversee service providers and handle servicing transfers, and must make information readily available to the personnel who deal with borrowers. The rule does not prescribe training, but it relies on servicing staff knowing these procedures. Loan originator qualification and training under the SAFE Act is covered separately in program 70.

references.title: 12 CFR 1024.38 General servicing policies, procedures, and requirements (Regulation X)
references.note: Servicers must keep policies and procedures that meet set objectives, including giving personnel ready access to the information they need to help borrowers.

programs.title: United States | Small Business Lending Data Collection (Section 1071, Regulation B Subpart B)
audience: Small business lenders and relationship managers
programs.why: Section 1071 requires covered lenders to collect and report data on small business credit applications, including demographic information, while keeping it away from decision makers where feasible. The CFPB revised the rule in May 2026, narrowing coverage, the small business definition and data points, and moved compliance to 1 January 2028. Staff who take applications must learn the collection and firewall procedures before that date.

references.title: Small Business Lending Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B), final rule
references.note: Revises coverage, the small business definition and the data points of the section 1071 rule; effective 30 June 2026 with compliance from 1 January 2028.

programs.title: United States | Bank Protection Act Security Program: Robbery and Cash Security Training
programs.why: Under the Bank Protection Act rules each bank names a security officer and keeps a written security program for every banking office. The program must give officers and employees initial and periodic training on their duties under the program and on how to behave during and after a robbery, burglary or larceny, alongside procedures for safeguarding cash and identifying offenders. The Federal Reserve rule is cited here; the OCC and FDIC have parallel rules.

references.title: 12 CFR 208.61 Bank security procedures (Regulation H, FRRS copy)
references.note: The security program must provide initial and periodic training for officers and employees on their security responsibilities and proper conduct during and after a robbery, burglary or larceny.

references.title: 12 CFR 21.3 Security program (OCC)
references.note: Parallel security program rule for national banks and federal savings associations.

references.title: 12 CFR 326.3 Security program (FDIC)
references.note: Parallel security program rule for FDIC-supervised institutions.

programs.title: United States | Remittance Transfer Rule (Regulation E Subpart B) and the Remittance Excise Tax
audience: Customer service staff handling transfer errors
programs.why: Banks that send consumer international transfers in the normal course of business are remittance transfer providers and must give prescribed disclosures, honour cancellation rights and follow error resolution procedures. From 1 January 2026 a federal excise tax applies to certain remittance transfers, and the IRS proposed implementing rules in April 2026. Front-line and operations staff need to know these duties; Regulation E does not set a training requirement.

references.title: 12 CFR 1005.30 Remittance transfer definitions (Regulation E)
references.note: A remittance transfer provider is anyone that provides remittance transfers for consumers in the normal course of business, whether or not the consumer holds an account there.

references.title: 12 CFR 1005.33 Procedures for resolving errors (Regulation E)
references.note: Defines errors in remittance transfers and the steps and time limits a provider must follow to investigate and remedy them.

references.title: Excise Tax on Remittance Transfers (proposed regulations)
references.note: Proposed rules and definitions for the excise tax on certain remittance transfers made after 31 December 2025, affecting remittance transfer providers.

programs.title: United States | Funds Availability and Check Collection (Regulation CC)
programs.why: Regulation CC sets the time limits for making deposited funds available, the exceptions and holds, and the notices customers must receive. Each bank must set procedures to comply and give every employee whose duties fall under the availability rules a statement of the procedures that apply to them. That duty targets the staff who take deposits and place holds, so it is classed as role-specific.

references.title: 12 CFR 229.19 Miscellaneous (Regulation CC, FRRS copy)
references.note: Under the heading on employee training and compliance, each bank must have procedures for complying with the availability rules and give each employee who performs those duties a statement of the procedures that apply to them.

programs.title: United States | Payments Fraud: Check, ACH, Wire and Instant Payments
programs.why: Check, ACH, wire and instant payment fraud has risen sharply, and in June 2025 the OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC asked for input on joint and separate actions to help banks and customers reduce it. No specific rule requires payments fraud training, but it supports the identity theft red flags program (program 29), suspicious activity reporting and Regulation E and CC duties.

references.title: Request for Information on Potential Actions To Address Payments Fraud
references.issuer: OCC, Federal Reserve Board and FDIC
references.note: Interagency request for comment on steps to mitigate check, ACH, wire and instant payments fraud; comments closed 18 September 2025.

programs.title: United States | Sexual Harassment Prevention Training (New York and Other State Laws)
audience: All employees in New York State
programs.why: Federal law does not require harassment training, and the EEOC rescinded its 2024 harassment guidance in 2026. Some states do require it. New York requires every employer to adopt a sexual harassment prevention policy and give each employee interactive training every year. Banks with staff in New York, and in other states with similar laws, must comply.

references.title: Employer Guide for Sexual Harassment Prevention
references.note: All New York employers must have a compliant policy and provide annual interactive training with a written notice.

references.title: Sexual Harassment Prevention Model Policy and Training
references.note: State model policy and model training that employers may adopt or exceed.

programs.title: United States | Call Reports and Regulatory Financial Reporting
programs.why: Insured banks must file reports of condition (Call Reports) in the form and with the content the agencies require, and errors or late filing bring penalties. In June 2026 nine agencies adopted joint data standards under the Financial Data Transparency Act, effective 1 October 2026, which do not change reporting duties yet but will guide future collections. No training is prescribed, but reporting staff must know the instructions.

references.title: Federal Deposit Insurance Act section 7 Assessments; Reports (FRRS copy)
references.note: Insured state nonmember banks must file reports of condition in the form and content the FDIC requires, with penalties for late or inaccurate reports; other agencies have parallel powers.

references.title: Financial Data Transparency Act Joint Data Standards (final rule)
references.issuer: OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, NCUA, CFPB, FHFA, CFTC, SEC and Treasury
references.note: Sets joint data standards for financial regulatory data; effective 1 October 2026 without changing reporting requirements until agencies act further.

programs.title: United States | FATCA (Chapter 4) Withholding and Form 1042-S Reporting
audience: Account opening staff collecting W-8/W-9 forms
programs.why: US banks act as withholding agents under FATCA. They must document foreign payees, withhold 30 percent on withholdable payments to non-participating foreign financial institutions and certain non-financial entities, and report on Form 1042-S. No training duty is set, but documentation errors cause withholding and penalty exposure, so role training is good practice.

references.title: Instructions for Form 1042-S (2026)
references.note: Chapter 3 and chapter 4 reporting duties for US and foreign withholding agents, including financial institutions.

references.title: Frequently asked questions (FAQs) FATCA compliance: Legal
references.note: IRS FAQs on FATCA legal requirements.

programs.title: United States | Annual Independent Audits and Audit Committees (FDI Act Section 36)
programs.why: Insured banks above the FDIC thresholds must produce annual audited financial statements and a management report on responsibilities and internal control, and keep an audit committee of independent outside directors. At large institutions the committee must include members with banking or related financial management expertise. The FDIC indexed these thresholds to inflation from 1 January 2026. The law sets expertise, not training, so this is classed as competence.

references.title: Federal Deposit Insurance Act section 36 Early Identification of Needed Improvements in Financial Management (FRRS copy)
references.note: Requires annual GAAP financial statements and a management report signed by the CEO and chief financial officer, and an independent audit committee that, at large institutions, includes members with banking or financial management expertise.

references.title: Adjusting and Indexing Certain Regulatory Thresholds (final rule)
references.note: Raises certain FDIC regulatory thresholds for inflation and indexes them for the future, effective 1 January 2026.

programs.title: United States | Volcker Rule Compliance Program (Regulation VV)
programs.why: Banking entities must keep a compliance program for the ban on proprietary trading and limits on covered fund investments, scaled to their activity. For entities with significant trading assets and liabilities the program must include training for trading personnel and managers and other appropriate staff so they can apply and enforce it. Entities with limited trading are exempt from the full program. The Federal Reserve version is cited; the OCC, FDIC, SEC and CFTC have matching rules.

references.title: 12 CFR 248.20 Program for compliance; reporting (Regulation VV, FRRS copy)
references.note: Banking entities, other than those with limited trading assets and liabilities, need a Volcker compliance program; for entities with significant trading assets and liabilities it must include training for trading personnel, managers and other appropriate staff.

programs.title: United States | Employee Securities Trading Reporting and Bank Securities Transaction Controls
audience: Trust and investment staff making recommendations
Staff who learn of customer securities orders
programs.why: State member banks that carry out securities transactions for customers must have written procedures that assign supervision of order and back-office staff, allocate orders fairly, and require officers and employees who make or learn of investment recommendations to report their own securities trades to the bank quarterly. These controls help prevent misuse of confidential information. The rule sets reporting and supervision duties rather than training.

references.title: 12 CFR 208.34 Recordkeeping and confirmation of certain securities transactions effected by state member banks (FRRS copy)
references.note: Written securities trading procedures must cover supervision of staff, fair allocation and crossing of orders, and quarterly reporting of personal securities trades by officers and employees with access to recommendations, within 10 days of quarter end.

programs.title: United States | Personal Financial Data Rights (CFPB Section 1033 Rule)
audience: Digital banking and API product teams
Third-party and data access risk staff
programs.why: The CFPB's 2024 rule requires covered banks to make consumer account data available to consumers and authorised third parties through compliant interfaces, with staggered compliance dates by asset size. In August 2025 the CFPB began reconsidering the rule, asking about who may act for a consumer, fees, and data security and privacy. Banks should track the outcome before investing in training; staff building and overseeing data access need to know the rule.

references.title: 12 CFR 1033.121 Compliance dates
references.note: Sets staggered initial compliance dates for data providers, starting 1 April 2026 for the largest depository institutions and running to 2030 for smaller covered banks.

references.title: Personal Financial Data Rights (CFPB rulemaking page)
references.note: Records the October 2024 final rule and the August 2025 advance notice on reconsidering it.

references.title: Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration (advance notice of proposed rulemaking)
references.note: Seeks comment on representatives, fees, and data security and privacy under section 1033; comments closed 21 October 2025.

programs.title: United States | Digital Identity Verification under the CIP Rule (Digital Credentials and TIN Exemption)
audience: Digital onboarding and account opening staff
programs.why: The Customer Identification Program rule lets banks verify identity by documentary or non-documentary methods under risk-based procedures. In 2025 the agencies allowed banks to obtain a customer's taxpayer identification number from a reliable third party instead of the customer, and in September 2026 they issued FAQs on using verifiable digital credentials such as mobile driver's licences. Staff running remote onboarding need to apply these updated procedures; no separate training rule applies.

references.title: SR 26-6 Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Treatment of Verifiable Digital Credentials Under the Customer Identification Program Rule
references.note: Interagency FAQs on using verifiable digital credentials, such as state mobile driver's licences, to verify natural person customers under the CIP rule.

references.title: SR 25-2 Order Granting an Exemption from the CIP Rule Requirement Related to Obtaining TIN Information from the Customer
references.note: Lets Federal Reserve-supervised banks obtain TIN information from a third-party source rather than the customer, provided the rest of the CIP rule is met.

programs.title: United States | AI Governance and Model Risk
audience: Data science and model development staff
programs.why: The 2026 interagency model risk guidance applies to traditional statistical models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, but leaves generative and agentic AI outside its scope and tells banks to govern them through their wider risk management. No US federal banking rule requires AI training. Training on model governance, validation and fair lending risk for AI tools is good practice; consumer credit decisions still need specific adverse action reasons under Regulation B.

references.title: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (attachment to SR 26-2)
references.issuer: Federal Reserve Board, OCC and FDIC
references.note: Generative and agentic AI are outside the guidance, which still applies to non-generative AI models; other tools are to be governed under the bank's general risk management.

notes: AML/CFT program reform: in April 2026 FinCEN withdrew its 2024 proposal and proposed a new effectiveness-based AML/CFT program rule. The OCC, FDIC and NCUA proposed parallel rules the same day (comments closed 9 June 2026) and the Federal Reserve proposed its own on 9 July 2026 (comments closed 8 September 2026). No final rule had been issued by early November 2026. Ongoing employee training stays one of four required pillars.

Corporate Transparency Act: a March 2025 interim final rule exempted US companies and US persons from BOI reporting. FinCEN's final rule, effective 14 August 2026, made this permanent, so only foreign reporting companies file. Banks' own beneficial ownership duty under 31 CFR 1010.230 continues.

In February 2026 FinCEN granted exceptive relief so that banks generally need not re-identify and re-verify beneficial owners each time an existing legal entity customer opens a new account, unless risk calls for it.
FinCEN proposed AML whistleblower incentive and protection rules on 1 April 2026. Awards will be paid once the rule is final.

The OCC proposed in December 2025 to raise the heightened standards threshold, including the director training requirement, from USD 50 billion to USD 700 billion in assets. No final rule had been published by early November 2026.

The CFPB cut back its supervision from 2025, focusing on depository institutions. In April 2026 it amended Regulation B to remove disparate impact liability (effective 21 July 2026) and updated its ECOA examination procedures. Consumer compliance training content should reflect these changes.

In June 2026 the Federal Reserve reposted the interagency operational resilience sound practices paper with references to reputational risk removed; the FDIC finalised a rule in April 2026 barring the use of reputation risk in supervision.
NYDFS Part 500, as amended in November 2023, phased in through November 2025. The annual awareness training with social engineering has applied since 2024.
The US does not take part in the OECD Common Reporting Standard, so program 181 (CRS) was not mapped. FATCA duties for US banks are those of withholding agents, not of FFIs under an FFI agreement.

Prudential changes in 2026: SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on model risk in April; the OCC rescinded its recovery planning guidelines from 1 May; the community bank leverage ratio fell to 8 percent from 1 July; capital proposals of March 2026 would recalibrate risk weights; and the stress capital buffer will average two years of stress tests from 1 December. The revised Section 1071 rule takes effect for compliance on 1 January 2028.
